title: Auth middleware with MongoDB
idea: `authenticate` is middleware that verifies the token, loads that user from MongoDB and sets `req.user`. Any failure ends the request with `401`.
points: `/login` finds the user by email, compares passwords with `bcrypt.compare`, then signs a token.
The token's `sub` claim holds the user's id.
`authenticate` verifies the token, then loads that user with `User.findById(sub)`.
A valid token for a deleted user still gets `401`: the lookup finds `null`.

messages.label: POST /login
messages.note: The client sends an email and a password as JSON.

messages.label: findOne({ email })
messages.note: Express checks that both values are strings, then looks the user up by email.

messages.label: 200 { token }
messages.note: The password matches the stored hash, so `jwt.sign` puts the user's id in `sub`.

messages.label: GET /me + token
messages.note: Every later request sends the token in the `Authorization` header.

messages.label: findById(sub)
messages.note: `authenticate` verifies the token, then loads the user that `sub` names.

messages.label: 200 { email }
messages.note: The query selects only `email`. `req.user` is set, `next()` runs and the route answers.

messages.label: GET /me, same token
messages.note: Later the account is deleted. The old token still verifies: signature and expiry are fine.

messages.label: findById(sub)
messages.note: `authenticate` looks the user up again, as it does on every request.

messages.label: null
messages.note: No document matches, so `findById` resolves to `null`.
`authenticate` ends the request. A valid token is not enough: the user must exist.

walk.text: A demo secret and a `User` model. `unique` asks MongoDB for a unique index on `email`.
`authenticate` reads the bearer token and verifies it, accepting only HS256. A bad token gets `401`.
Next, load the user from MongoDB, selecting only `email`. No user means `401`; otherwise `next()` runs.
Before any query, both fields must be strings: an object could act as a query operator.
Look up the email, compare the hash, then sign a token whose `sub` is the id.
Seed one user and call the routes. The last call reuses the token after deleting the user.

pitfalls: Check types before querying: an object in place of a string becomes a query operator.
Use one message for unknown email and wrong password; two messages reveal which emails exist.
Keep `passwordHash` off `req.user`: select only the fields your routes need.

quiz.why: The token still verifies, so `sub` matches the id. But the user is gone: `findById` resolves to `null`.

takeaway: A valid token proves who signed it; the database says whether the user exists.

starters: Why query MongoDB on every request if the token is signed?
